title: Ants on a stick
objectives: Use symmetry to dissolve a complicated set-up.

screens.title: Two ants
screens.prose: Ant A starts at 0.2 m walking right; ant B at 0.7 m walking left. Both walk 1 m a minute. When they meet they turn round. Slide the time.
screens.question: When has the last ant fallen off, in minutes?

hints.text: Ignore the labels and watch the two dots.
One dot moves like $0.2 + t$, the other like $0.7 - t$.
They leave at $t = 0.8$ (right end) and $t = 0.7$ (left end).

feedback.correct: At 0.8 minutes, when the dot from 0.2 m reaches the right end.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Watch when each dot leaves, not which ant it is.

byKey.first: That is when the first ant falls. The other is still walking.
byKey.meet: That is when they meet and turn.
byKey.whole: No ant walks the whole stick here.

explain.text: After the bounce, A walks the path B would have walked, and B walks A’s. The two dots move exactly as if the ants passed through. So the stick is empty when the later path ends: $1 - 0.2 = 0.8$ minutes.

screens.title: A hundred ants
screens.prose: Now 100 ants at random points of the stick, each facing left or right at random. Bouncing does not change the set of dots, so each dot leaves when its pass-through ghost would.

derive.caption: t = {{fixed(t, 2)}} min. The dots move as if the ants passed through each other.

screens.question: What is the expected time until the last ant falls, in minutes? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: A ghost at $x$ leaves at $x$ or at $1 - x$: a uniform time.
The last ant falls at the largest of 100 uniform times.
The largest of $n$ uniforms averages $\tfrac{n}{n + 1}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The last fall is the maximum of 100 uniform exit times.

byKey.half: That is one ant on average. The last of 100 waits for the slowest.
byKey.one: One minute is the most it can take, not the average.

explain.text: Each ghost leaves at a uniform time on $[0, 1]$, whatever the others do. The last fall is their maximum, averaging $\tfrac{100}{101}$, from l11. No collision needs to be drawn.

screens.title: From the two ends
screens.prose: Two ants start at the two ends of the 1 m stick. They walk towards each other at 1 m a minute.
screens.question: When does the last ant fall, in minutes?

hints.text: Replace the bounce with passing through.
Each ghost walks the whole stick.
Each takes 1 minute.

feedback.correct: They meet at 30 seconds and both fall at 1 minute.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Let the ants pass through each other.

byKey.meet: That is when they meet. Each then walks back half a metre.
byKey.double: Each ant walks only 1 m in all: half there, half back.

explain.text: They meet in the middle after 30 seconds and turn. Each walks back half a metre to the end it came from. Both fall at 1 minute, just as ghosts walking the whole stick would.

screens.title: The fly and the trains
screens.prose: Two trains 100 miles apart head towards each other at 50 mph each. A fly at 75 mph zigzags between them until they meet.

state.caption: Miles apart: 100. Each train 50 mph, the fly 75 mph.

screens.question: How far does the fly fly, in miles?

hints.text: Do not add up the zigzags.
How long until the trains meet?
They close at 100 mph, so 1 hour: the fly does 75 miles.

feedback.correct: The trains meet in 1 hour, so the fly covers 75 miles.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the time first, then the fly’s distance.

byKey.first-leg: That is the first leg alone: 100 miles at a closing speed of 125 mph. There are infinitely many more.
byKey.gap: That is the gap between the trains, not the fly’s path.
byKey.sum: You doubled the fly’s distance. It flies for one hour at 75 mph.

explain.text: The trains close at 100 mph, so they meet in one hour. The fly flies for that hour at 75 mph: 75 miles. Describing it by time removes the infinite series.

screens.title: Draw the collisions?
screens.prose: Back to 100 ants on a 1 m stick at 1 m a minute. A candidate starts drawing the first few collisions to see how long the worst case lasts.
screens.question: What is the longest the last ant can take to fall?

options.text: It depends on how the collisions fall, so you must trace them
options.why: That is the trap. Swap labels at each bounce and every ghost walks straight off within a minute.

options.text: Up to 100 minutes, as each bounce sends an ant back
options.why: Bounces swap which ant follows which path. No path is longer than the stick.
A ghost never turns round. It walks at most 1 m.

hints.text: Swap the labels at every collision.
Every dot then walks straight.
A straight walk off a 1 m stick takes at most 1 minute.

feedback.correct: At most 1 minute, whatever the start.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Describe the ants as ghosts that pass through.

byKey.b: You reached for the collisions. In an interview that costs the time. Ghosts walk straight, so 1 minute is the most.

explain.text: With labels swapped at each bounce, every dot walks straight. A straight walk leaves a 1 m stick within 1 minute. The worst case is an ant at one end facing the other.

screens.title: Change the description
screens.prose:
Each puzzle got easy once we described it another way. Bouncing ants are ghosts that pass through, because only the **set** of positions matters. The fly is a time, not a series.

$$T_{\text{last}} = \max_i \, (\text{ghost } i\text{’s exit time})$$
screens.question: One ant at a random point, facing a random way. When does it fall, on average?

options.why: One ant is the edge case: its exit time is uniform on $[0, 1]$, so it averages a half.
You halved twice. The distance to the end it faces is already uniform on $[0, 1]$.

hints.text: Its exit time is $x$ or $1 - x$.
Either way it is uniform on $[0, 1]$.
Mean $\tfrac12$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Its exit time is uniform on $[0, 1]$.

explain.text: With one ant there are no collisions at all. Its exit time is uniform, mean $\tfrac12 = \tfrac{1}{1 + 1}$. The edge case checks the formula.

screens.title: Why ghosts work
screens.prose: Say why bouncing is the same as passing through. Put the argument in order.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. Leave out the line that does not belong.

lines.text: When two ants meet, both turn round at the same point.
Swap their labels at that moment: the two dots carry on as if they had passed.
So at every time the set of positions is the set of pass-through ghosts.
The stick is empty when the last ghost leaves: the largest exit time.
So each ant falls when its own ghost does.

hints.text: Start at one collision.
What does a label swap change?
Collision, swap, same set, last exit.

feedback.correct: The set of dots is the same, so the last exit is the last fall.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start at a single collision.

byKey.d1: Labels are swapped at each bounce, so ant A follows other ghosts’ paths. Only the set of fall times is easy.
byKey.left-out: Every line except the one about each ant’s own ghost belongs.

explain.text: A bounce and a pass leave the same two dots in the same places. Only the names differ. So any question about the set of positions, or the last fall, is a ghost question.

screens.title: Drill
screens.prose: Three new puzzles at about 3 minutes each, 9 in all. Keep your own time. Ants walk 1 m a minute on a 1 m stick. Four decimal places.
screens.question: Fill in the three answers.

rows: 10 ants at random points facing random ways. Expected time until all fall?
Ants at 0.3 m (right) and 0.6 m (left). When does the last fall?
3 ants walk right from the left half, 2 walk left from the right half. How many collisions?

hints.text: Ghosts for all three.
Each right-walker’s ghost crosses each left-walker’s ghost once.
$\tfrac{10}{11}$; ghosts leave at 0.7 and 0.6; $3 \times 2$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r0c1: Check the first: the largest of 10 uniform exit times averages $\tfrac{10}{11}$.
byKey.r1c1: Check the second: the ghost from 0.3 m leaves the right end at $t = 0.7$.
byKey.r2c1: Check the third: every right-walking ghost meets every left-walking ghost once, $3 \times 2$.

explain.text: Ten ants: $\tfrac{10}{11} \approx 0.9091$. The two ants: ghosts leave at $0.7$ and $0.6$, so $0.7$. Collisions are ghost crossings: each of 3 right-walkers crosses each of 2 left-walkers, 6 in all.

screens.title: Follow-up: a longer stick
screens.prose: You said $\tfrac{100}{101}$ minutes. The interviewer asks: and on a 2 m stick, still at 1 m a minute?
screens.question: What is the expected time until the last of 100 ants falls? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: Each exit time is now uniform on $[0, 2]$.
Scale the 1 m answer.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Every time doubles with the stick.

byKey.same: That is the 1 m stick. Every exit time doubles.
byKey.two: Two minutes is the most it can take, not the average.

explain.text: Doubling the stick doubles every exit time. So the answer doubles: $\tfrac{200}{101}$. Saying the scaling argument is faster than redoing the sum.

screens.title: Netting fills
screens.prose: A desk starts flat. It gets buys of 300, 200 and 500 shares and sells of 400 and 100. The order of the fills is lost.
screens.question: What can you state without knowing the order?

options.text: The largest position held during the day
options.why: That depends on the order, like the path of one labelled ant. Only the net is order-free.

options.text: Whether the desk was ever short
options.why: Selling 400 first would make it short; buying first would not. The order matters.
The net is a sum, and sums ignore order.

hints.text: Which number is a plain sum?
Buys minus sells.

feedback.correct: The net, $+500$, ignores the order, like the set of ants.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the one quantity that is a plain sum.

explain.text: The closing position is buys minus sells, 500, in any order. The path through the day depends on the order. As with the ants, ask what the question really depends on.

screens.title: The frog
screens.prose: A question reported at trading firms: a frog climbs 10 steps, jumping one or two at a time. Count by the last jump, as in graphs-dp l13 (Counting ways to climb).

state.caption: Count by the last jump: the frog arrives from $n - 1$ or from $n - 2$.

screens.question: In how many ways can the frog reach step 10?

hints.text: The last jump is one step or two.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the two previous counts each time.

byKey.power: You allowed a jump choice at every step. A two-step jump uses two steps at once.
byKey.nine: That is step 9. Add one more term.

explain.text: Describing a climb by its last jump splits it into the climbs to $n - 1$ and to $n - 2$. So $w(n) = w(n - 1) + w(n - 2)$, giving 89 at $n = 10$. Changing the description again does the work.

ideas: Bouncing ants are ghosts that pass through: the set of positions is the same at every time.
The last ant falls at the largest ghost exit time, $\tfrac{n}{n + 1}$ on average for random starts.
Change the description until the complication goes: a time, not a series; a last jump, not a path.
summary.trap: Drawing the collisions one by one. Ghosts walk straight, so the answer needs none of them.

quiz.prose: 100 ants at random on a 1 m stick, bouncing on collision. One ant is painted red.
quiz.question: When does the red ant fall?

options.text: It depends on the other ants’ positions and directions

options.why: Bounces swap which path it follows. The red ant takes over other ghosts’ paths.
That is the last fall. One named ant may fall much sooner.

feedback.correct: Only the set of fall times is easy; one named ant needs the others.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Bounces swap labels between paths.

explain.text: The ghost trick gives the set of fall times, not who falls when. The red ant keeps its place in the left-to-right order. So its fall depends on where the others start and which way they face.

quiz.prose: Four ants walk right from the left half of a stick and four walk left from the right half.
quiz.question: How many collisions happen?

feedback.correct: Each right-walker meets each left-walker once: 16.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count ghost crossings.

byKey.eight: You added the two groups. Each pair of opposite walkers meets once, so multiply.
byKey.pairs: You counted all pairs of ants. Ants walking the same way never meet.

explain.text: A collision is a crossing of a right ghost and a left ghost. Every such pair crosses once: $4 \times 4 = 16$.

quiz.prose: Two cyclists 60 miles apart ride towards each other at 30 mph each. A bird flies between them at 90 mph until they meet.
quiz.question: How far does the bird fly, in miles?

feedback.correct: They meet in 1 hour, so the bird flies 90 miles.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the time until they meet.

byKey.gap: That is the gap between the cyclists.
byKey.first: That is only the first leg. Use the total time instead.

explain.text: The cyclists close at 60 mph and meet in an hour. The bird flies 90 miles in that hour.
